verses.text: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked the LORD, “Which of us should go up first to fight the Canaanites?”
The LORD answered, “Judah will go up. I've handed the land over to them.”
Judah said to their fellow tribe Simeon, “Come with us into the land assigned to us so we can fight the Canaanites. Then we'll go with you into the land assigned to you.” So Simeon went with Judah.
When Judah went up, the LORD handed the Canaanites and Perizzites over to them. They struck down ten thousand men at Bezek.
They found Adoni-Bezek at Bezek and fought him there, defeating the Canaanites and Perizzites.
Adoni-Bezek ran, but they chased him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes.
Adoni-Bezek said, “Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off used to gather scraps under my table. God has done to me what I did to them.” They took him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah fought against Jerusalem, captured it, put its people to the sword, and set the city on fire.
Then Judah went down to fight the Canaanites living in the hill country, the south, and the lowlands.
Judah went against the Canaanites of Hebron, which used to be called Kiriath Arba. They struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
From there they went against the people of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath Sepher.
Caleb said, “I'll give my daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever attacks Kiriath Sepher and takes it.”
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it. So Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah in marriage.
When Achsah came to Othniel, she got him to ask her father for a field. She got down from her donkey, and Caleb asked, “What would you like?”
She said, “Give me a blessing. You've given me land in the south, so please give me springs of water too.” Caleb gave her the upper and lower springs.
The descendants of the Kenite, Moses' brother-in-law, left the City of Palms with the people of Judah. They went into the wilderness of Judah south of Arad and settled there among the people.
Judah went with their fellow tribe Simeon, and together they struck the Canaanites living at Zephath and destroyed the town completely. It was renamed Hormah.
Judah also took Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, with the land around each city.
The LORD was with Judah, and Judah drove out the people of the hill country. They couldn't drive out the people of the valley because those people had iron chariots.
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and Caleb drove out the three descendants of Anak.
Benjamin didn't drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem. The Jebusites still live there with the people of Benjamin today.
Joseph's descendants also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them.
They sent scouts to Bethel, which used to be called Luz.
The scouts saw a man coming out of the city. They told him, “Please show us the way into the city, and we'll treat you kindly.”
He showed them the entrance. They put the city to the sword, but they let the man and his whole family go.
He went into Hittite country, built a city, and named it Luz. That's still its name today.
Manasseh didn't drive out the people of Beth Shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, or Megiddo, or the people in their surrounding towns. The Canaanites were determined to stay in the land.
When Israel grew strong, they made the Canaanites do forced labor, but they didn't drive them out completely.
Ephraim didn't drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer. The Canaanites stayed there among them.
Zebulun didn't drive out the people of Kitron or Nahalol. The Canaanites lived among them and were made to do forced labor.
Asher didn't drive out the people of Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, or Rehob.
So the people of Asher lived among the Canaanites who were already in the land, because they hadn't driven them out.
Naphtali didn't drive out the people of Beth Shemesh or Beth Anath. They lived among the Canaanites who were already in the land, but made the people of those two towns do forced labor.
The Amorites pushed the people of Dan into the hill country and wouldn't let them come down into the valley.
The Amorites were determined to stay in Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim. But Joseph's descendants gained the upper hand and made them do forced labor.
The Amorite border ran from the Akrabbim Pass, from the Rock and upward.
The LORD's angel went up from Gilgal to Bochim and said, “I brought you out of Egypt and into the land I swore to give your ancestors. I told you, ‘I'll never break my covenant with you.
Don't make a treaty with the people living in this land. Tear down their altars.’ But you haven't listened to me. Why did you do this?
So I also said, ‘I won't drive them out ahead of you. They'll be thorns in your sides, and their gods will trap you.’”
When the LORD's angel said all this to the Israelites, the people cried out and wept.
They named the place Bochim and offered sacrifices to the LORD there.
After Joshua sent the people away, the Israelites each went to take possession of the land they'd received as their inheritance.
The people served the LORD throughout Joshua's life and throughout the lives of the elders who outlived him and had seen all the great things the LORD did for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the LORD's servant, died at 110 years old.
They buried him within his own land at Timnath Heres in Ephraim's hill country, north of Mount Gaash.
After that whole generation died and joined their ancestors, another generation grew up that didn't know the LORD or what he'd done for Israel.
The Israelites did what was evil in the LORD's sight and served the Baals.
They abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of Egypt. They followed and bowed down to other gods worshiped by the peoples around them, and they made the LORD angry.
They turned away from the LORD and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.
The LORD's anger burned against Israel. He handed them over to raiders who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all around them, and they could no longer stand against them.
Whenever they went out, the LORD's hand worked against them and brought disaster, just as he'd told them and sworn to them. They were in terrible distress.
The LORD raised up judges who rescued them from the hands of the people plundering them.

But they refused to listen to their judges. They were unfaithful to the LORD, chasing after other gods and bowing down to them. They quickly abandoned the way their ancestors had lived, obeying the LORD's commands. They didn't follow their example.

Whenever the LORD raised up a judge, he was with that judge and rescued the people from their enemies for as long as the judge lived. The LORD was grieved when they groaned under the people oppressing and mistreating them.

But when the judge died, they went back to their old ways and acted even worse than their ancestors, following, serving, and bowing down to other gods. They wouldn't give up their practices or their stubborn ways.
The LORD's anger burned against Israel. He said, “This nation has broken the covenant I commanded their ancestors to keep and hasn't listened to me.
So I won't drive out any more of the nations Joshua left behind when he died.
I'll use them to test Israel and see whether they'll keep to the LORD's way and live by it as their ancestors did.”
So the LORD let those nations remain instead of driving them out right away. He didn't hand them over to Joshua.
Here are the nations the LORD left in place to test the Israelites who hadn't experienced the wars in Canaan.
He left them there so later generations of Israelites who had never known war would learn what it was like.
They were the five Philistine rulers, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites living in the mountains of Lebanon from Mount Baal Hermon to the entrance of Hamath.
The LORD left them there to test Israel and see whether the people would listen to the commands he'd given their ancestors through Moses.
The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
They married their daughters, gave their own daughters in marriage to their sons, and served their gods.
The Israelites did what was evil in the LORD's sight. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.
The LORD's anger burned against Israel. He sold them into the hands of King Cushan Rishathaim of Mesopotamia, and the Israelites served him for eight years.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD, he raised up someone to rescue them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.
The LORD's Spirit came upon Othniel, and he became Israel's judge. He went to war, and the LORD handed King Cushan Rishathaim of Mesopotamia over to him. Othniel defeated him.
The land had peace for forty years. Then Othniel son of Kenaz died.
The Israelites again did what was evil in the LORD's sight. Because of what they'd done, the LORD made King Eglon of Moab strong against Israel.
Eglon gathered the Ammonites and Amalekites with him, attacked Israel, and took the City of Palms.
The Israelites served King Eglon of Moab for eighteen years.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD, he raised up a rescuer for them: Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjaminite. The Israelites sent him to deliver their tribute to King Eglon of Moab.
Ehud made himself a short, double-edged sword and wore it out of sight under his clothes.
He delivered the tribute to King Eglon of Moab, who was a very heavy man.
When Ehud finished delivering the tribute, he sent away the people who had carried it.
Ehud himself turned back at the stone idols near Gilgal and said, “I have a private message for you, King.” Eglon called for silence, and everyone with him left the room.
Ehud approached Eglon, who was sitting alone in his cool upstairs room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you.” Eglon stood up from his seat.
Ehud drew his sword and stabbed him.
The blade went all the way through, and the handle sank in after it. Ehud left the sword where it was.
Ehud went out onto the porch and shut and locked the doors of the upstairs room behind him.
After Ehud left, Eglon's servants came and found the upstairs doors locked. They said, “He must be relieving himself in the upstairs room.”
They waited until they felt embarrassed. When he still didn't open the doors, they took the key and unlocked them. Their master was lying dead on the floor.
While they waited, Ehud got away. He passed the stone idols and escaped to Seirah.
When he arrived, he blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down from the hills with him, and he led them.
He told them, “Follow me. The LORD has handed your enemies, the Moabites, over to you.” They followed him, took control of the Jordan crossings, and let no Moabite cross.
They struck down about ten thousand Moabite men, all strong and capable fighters. None escaped.
That day Israel subdued Moab, and the land had peace for eighty years.
After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. He struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad, and he too rescued Israel.
After Ehud died, the Israelites again did what was evil in the LORD's sight.
The LORD sold them into the hands of King Jabin of Canaan, who ruled in Hazor. His army commander was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD for help. Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots and had ruthlessly oppressed Israel for twenty years.
Deborah, a prophet and the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.
She stayed under Deborah's Palm between Ramah and Bethel in Ephraim's hill country. The Israelites came to her to settle their disputes.

She sent for Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali. She said, “Hasn't the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you to go to Mount Tabor and lead ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun with you?
He said, ‘I'll draw Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, with his chariots and troops to the Kishon River, where I'll hand him over to you.’”
Barak said, “If you go with me, I'll go. If you don't, I won't.”
“I'll go with you,” she answered. “But you won't get the honor for this campaign, because the LORD will hand Sisera over to a woman.” Deborah got up and went with Barak to Kedesh.
At Kedesh, Barak called out the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. Ten thousand men followed him, and Deborah went with him.
Heber the Kenite had moved away from his people, the descendants of Hobab, Moses' brother-in-law. He set up his tent as far away as the oak at Zaanannim near Kedesh.
Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor.
He called out all nine hundred of his iron chariots and all his troops from Harosheth of the Gentiles and brought them to the Kishon River.
Deborah told Barak, “Go! Today the LORD has handed Sisera over to you. Hasn't the LORD gone ahead of you?” Barak went down Mount Tabor with ten thousand men behind him.
The LORD threw Sisera, his chariots, and his whole army into confusion as Barak came against them with the sword. Sisera abandoned his chariot and ran away on foot.
Barak chased the chariots and the army to Harosheth of the Gentiles. Sisera's entire army fell by the sword. None survived.
Sisera ran to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because King Jabin of Hazor was at peace with Heber's household.
Jael went out to meet Sisera and said, “Come inside, my lord. Come in and don't be afraid.” He came into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.
He told her, “Please give me some water. I'm thirsty.” She opened a container of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him again.
He told her, “Stand at the entrance. If anyone comes and asks whether there's a man in here, say no.”
While Sisera slept deeply, Jael, Heber's wife, went quietly to him and killed him with a tent peg and hammer.
As Barak came looking for Sisera, Jael went out to meet him. “Come, I'll show you the man you're looking for.” He went in with her and saw Sisera lying dead with the tent peg in his head.
That day God subdued King Jabin of Canaan before the Israelites.
Israel grew stronger and stronger against King Jabin of Canaan until they destroyed him.
That day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song.
“Israel's leaders stepped forward, and the people volunteered freely. Praise the LORD!
Listen, you kings! Pay attention, you rulers! I will sing to the LORD. I'll sing praises to the LORD, the God of Israel.
LORD, when you came out of Seir and marched from the fields of Edom, the earth shook. The sky poured down rain, and the clouds spilled water.
The mountains shook in the presence of the LORD. Even Sinai shook before the LORD, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath and in the days of Jael, the main roads were empty. Travelers kept to the back roads.
Leaders disappeared from Israel until I, Deborah, rose up, until I rose as a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods, and war came to the gates. Was a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart is with Israel's leaders who stepped forward willingly among the people. Praise the LORD!
Speak up, you who ride white donkeys, you who sit on fine carpets, and you who travel on foot.
Away from the sound of archers, at the watering places, people will tell of the LORD's righteous acts, how he ruled with justice in Israel. Then the LORD's people went down to the gates.
‘Wake up, wake up, Deborah! Wake up, wake up, sing a song! Get up, Barak son of Abinoam, and lead your captives away!’
Then the survivors of the nobles and the people came down. The LORD came down for me against the mighty.
From Ephraim came those rooted in Amalek. Benjamin, you followed with your people. Leaders came down from Machir. From Zebulun came those who carried the commander's staff.
Issachar's leaders were with Deborah. Issachar went with Barak, rushing into the valley right behind him. By Reuben's streams there were great resolutions of heart.
Why did you stay among the sheepfolds? Was it to hear the shepherds whistle for their flocks? By Reuben's streams there was much searching of heart.
Gilead stayed across the Jordan. Why did Dan stay with the ships? Asher sat still by the seashore and stayed near its inlets.
Zebulun risked their lives to the point of death, and so did Naphtali on the heights of the battlefield.
The kings came to fight. The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, and they took no silver as plunder.
The stars fought from the sky. From their courses they fought against Sisera.
The Kishon River swept them away, that ancient river, the Kishon. March on, my soul, with strength!
Then the horses' hooves thundered as their strong steeds galloped on and on.
‘Curse Meroz,’ said the LORD's angel. ‘Curse its people bitterly, because they didn't come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.’
Blessed above women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. Blessed above all women who live in tents is she.
He asked for water, and she gave him milk. She brought him butter in a bowl fit for a ruler.
She reached for a tent peg and a workman's hammer. She struck Sisera and killed him with a blow to the head.
At her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still. At her feet he sank and fell. Where he sank, there he fell dead.
Sisera's mother looked through the window and cried out through the lattice. ‘Why is his chariot taking so long? Why haven't I heard the wheels of his chariots?’
Her wisest ladies answered her, and she kept repeating the answer to herself.
‘They must have found plunder and be dividing it up: a woman or two for each man, and for Sisera some dyed clothes, embroidered clothes, cloth embroidered on both sides to wear around the neck.’
May all your enemies perish like that, LORD. May those who love you be like the sun rising in its strength.” Then the land had peace for forty years.
The Israelites did what was evil in the LORD's sight, so he handed them over to Midian for seven years.
Midian overpowered Israel. Because of the Midianites, the Israelites made shelters in the mountains, using caves and strongholds to hide.
Whenever Israel planted crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and peoples from the east came up against them.
They camped against Israel and destroyed the crops as far as Gaza. They left Israel without food, sheep, cattle, or donkeys.
They came with their livestock and tents, swarming in like locusts. There were too many people and camels to count, and they came to ruin the land.
Midian left Israel desperate and poor, so the Israelites cried out to the LORD.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD because of Midian,
the LORD sent a prophet, who said, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I brought you up out of Egypt and freed you from slavery.
I rescued you from the Egyptians and from everyone who oppressed you. I drove them out ahead of you and gave you their land.
I told you, “I am the LORD your God. Don't fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you live.” But you haven't listened to me.’”
The LORD's angel came and sat under an oak at Ophrah that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite. Joash's son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.
The LORD's angel appeared to him and said, “The LORD is with you, mighty warrior!”

Gideon said, “Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened? Where are all the wonders our ancestors told us about when they said, ‘Didn't the LORD bring us up out of Egypt?’ Now the LORD has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian.”
The LORD looked at him and said, “Go with the strength you have and rescue Israel from Midian. I'm the one sending you.”
Gideon answered, “Please, Lord, how can I rescue Israel? My clan is the poorest in Manasseh, and I'm the least important person in my father's household.”
The LORD told him, “I'll be with you. You'll strike down the Midianites as if they were a single man.”
Gideon said, “If I've found favor with you, give me a sign that it's really you speaking to me.
Please stay until I come back with my gift and set it before you.” He answered, “I'll wait until you return.”

Gideon went inside and prepared a young goat and flatbread made without yeast from an ephah of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot and brought them out under the oak to present them.
God's angel told him, “Set the meat and the flatbread on this rock and pour out the broth.” Gideon did it.
The LORD's angel touched the meat and the bread with the tip of his staff. Fire rose out of the rock and consumed both, and the LORD's angel disappeared from sight.
Gideon realized it was the LORD's angel and cried, “Oh, Lord GOD! I've seen the LORD's angel face to face!”
The LORD told him, “Peace to you. Don't be afraid. You won't die.”
Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and named it “The LORD Is Peace.” It's still there today at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
That night the LORD told him, “Take your father's second bull, the seven-year-old one. Tear down your father's altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.
Then build a proper altar to the LORD your God on top of this stronghold. Offer the second bull as a burnt offering, using the wood from the Asherah pole you cut down.”
Gideon took ten of his servants and did what the LORD had told him. He was afraid of his family and the townsmen, so he did it at night instead of in daylight.
When the townsmen got up early the next morning, they saw that Baal's altar had been torn down, the Asherah pole beside it had been cut down, and the second bull had been offered on the new altar.
They asked one another, “Who did this?” After asking around and looking into it, they said, “Gideon son of Joash did it.”
The townsmen told Joash, “Bring your son out so he can die. He tore down Baal's altar and cut down the Asherah pole next to it.”

Joash said to everyone standing against him, “Are you going to fight Baal's case for him? Are you going to save him? Anyone who fights his case should be put to death by morning. If Baal is a god, let him defend himself, since somebody tore down his altar.”
That day Joash named Gideon Jerub-Baal, saying, “Let Baal defend himself against him, because he tore down Baal's altar.”
Then the Midianites, Amalekites, and peoples from the east joined forces, crossed over, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel.
But the LORD's Spirit came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet. The clan of Abiezer rallied behind him.
He sent messengers throughout Manasseh, and they rallied behind him too. He also sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came up to meet them.
Gideon said to God, “If you're really going to rescue Israel through me, as you said,
I'll put a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If dew settles only on the fleece and the rest of the ground stays dry, I'll know you'll rescue Israel through me, as you said.”
That's what happened. Gideon got up early the next day, squeezed the fleece, and wrung out enough dew to fill a bowl.
Gideon said to God, “Please don't be angry with me. Let me speak just once more and test the fleece one last time. This time, let the fleece stay dry and let there be dew all over the ground.”
God did exactly that that night. Only the fleece stayed dry, and there was dew all over the ground.
Jerubbaal, also known as Gideon, got up early with everyone who was with him. They camped beside the spring of Harod. Midian's camp lay north of them in the valley near the hill of Moreh.
The LORD told Gideon, “You have too many people with you for me to hand Midian over to them. Israel might boast against me and say, ‘We saved ourselves.’
So announce to everyone, ‘Anyone who is trembling with fear can go home and leave Mount Gilead.’” Twenty-two thousand went home, and ten thousand stayed.

The LORD told Gideon, “There are still too many. Bring them down to the water, and I'll test them for you there. The ones I tell you to take will go with you, and the ones I tell you to leave will stay behind.”
Gideon took the people down to the water. The LORD told him, “Separate everyone who laps the water with his tongue like a dog from everyone who kneels down to drink.”
Three hundred men lapped the water, bringing it to their mouths with their hands. Everyone else knelt down to drink.
The LORD told Gideon, “I'll use the three hundred who lapped the water to rescue you and hand the Midianites over to you. Let everyone else go home.”
The men took their food and trumpets. Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites back to their tents but kept the three hundred. The Midianite camp was below him in the valley.
That night the LORD told Gideon, “Get up and go down into the camp. I've handed it over to you.
If you're afraid to go down, take your servant Purah with you.
Listen to what they're saying there. Afterward you'll have the courage to go down into the camp.” So Gideon and Purah went down to the edge of the armed camp.
The Midianites, Amalekites, and peoples from the east filled the valley like a swarm of locusts. Their camels were as countless as grains of sand on the seashore.
When Gideon got there, a man was telling another man about a dream. “I dreamed a loaf of barley bread rolled into the Midianite camp. It hit a tent so hard it flipped over and lay flat.”
The other man answered, “That can only mean the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has handed Midian and its entire army over to him.”
When Gideon heard the dream and what it meant, he bowed in worship. Then he returned to Israel's camp and said, “Get up! The LORD has handed the Midianite army over to you.”
He divided the three hundred men into three groups and gave each man a trumpet and an empty jar with a torch inside.
He told them, “Watch me and follow my lead. When I reach the edge of the camp, do what I do.
When I and the men with me blow our trumpets, blow yours all around the camp and shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’”
Gideon and his hundred men reached the edge of the camp at the start of the middle watch, just after the guards changed. They blew their trumpets and smashed the jars they were carrying.
All three groups blew their trumpets and smashed their jars. Holding torches in their left hands and trumpets in their right, they shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!”
They held their positions around the camp while the whole army ran. The men shouted and sent them fleeing.

When the three hundred trumpets sounded, the LORD turned the swords of the men in the camp against one another throughout the army. The army fled as far as Beth Shittah toward Zererah and the edge of Abel Meholah near Tabbath.
Israelite men from Naphtali, Asher, and all of Manasseh gathered and went after Midian.

Gideon sent messengers through Ephraim's hill country, calling on the men to come down against Midian and seize the waters as far as Beth Barah and the Jordan. The men of Ephraim gathered and took control of those waters.

They captured two Midianite leaders, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the Rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the Winepress of Zeeb while they chased the Midianites. Then they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
The men of Ephraim confronted Gideon sharply. “Why did you treat us like this? Why didn't you call us when you went to fight Midian?”
He answered, “What have I done compared with what you've done? Aren't the grapes Ephraim picks after the harvest better than Abiezer's whole harvest?
God handed the Midianite leaders Oreb and Zeeb over to you. What did I manage to do compared with that?” When he said this, their anger toward him cooled.
Gideon and the three hundred men with him reached the Jordan and crossed it. They were exhausted, but they kept up the pursuit.
Gideon asked the men of Succoth, “Please give my men some bread. They're exhausted, and I'm chasing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
Succoth's leaders answered, “Do you already have Zebah and Zalmunna in your hands? Why should we feed your army?”
Gideon said, “When the LORD hands Zebah and Zalmunna over to me, I'll tear your flesh with thorns and briars from the wilderness.”
From there Gideon went up to Penuel and made the same request. The men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had.
He told the men of Penuel, “When I come back safely, I'll tear down this tower.”
Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that was left of the eastern army. A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had fallen.
Gideon went up along the route of the people living in tents east of Nobah and Jogbehah. He attacked when the army thought it was safe.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but Gideon chased them and captured both kings of Midian. The whole army was thrown into confusion.
Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the Heres Pass.
He caught a young man from Succoth and questioned him. The young man listed Succoth's leaders and elders for him, seventy-seven men in all.

Gideon went to the men of Succoth and said, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, the men you mocked me about when you asked, ‘Do you already have them in your hands? Why should we give bread to your exhausted men?’”
He took the city elders and used wilderness thorns and briars to punish the men of Succoth.
He also tore down Penuel's tower and killed the men of that town.
Then he asked Zebah and Zalmunna, “What were the men you killed at Tabor like?” They said, “They were like you. Every one of them looked like a king's son.”
Gideon said, “They were my brothers, my own mother's sons. As surely as the LORD lives, if you had spared them, I would spare you now.”
He told his firstborn, Jether, “Get up and kill them.” But the boy didn't draw his sword. He was still young and afraid.
Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up and do it yourself. A man's strength matches the man.” Gideon got up, killed them, and took the crescent ornaments from their camels' necks.
The Israelites said to Gideon, “Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson. You rescued us from Midian.”
Gideon answered, “I won't rule over you, and my son won't rule over you. The LORD will rule over you.”
Then Gideon said, “I do have one request. Each of you give me an earring from what you took.” The defeated men wore gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites.
“We'll gladly give them,” they said. They spread out a garment, and each man threw in the earrings he'd taken.

The gold earrings Gideon asked for weighed seventeen hundred shekels. That was in addition to the crescents, the pendants, the purple clothes worn by the Midianite kings, and the chains around their camels' necks.
Gideon made an ephod from the gold and put it in his town of Ophrah. All Israel was unfaithful to God there by going after it, and it became a trap for Gideon and his household.
Midian was subdued before the Israelites and never rose up against them again. The land had peace for forty years in Gideon's time.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went back to live in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons of his own, because he had many wives.
His concubine in Shechem also gave him a son, whom he named Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age. He was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites again turned away from the LORD to follow the Baals. They made Baal Berith their god.
They forgot the LORD their God, who had rescued them from all their enemies on every side.
They also failed to show kindness to the family of Jerubbaal, also known as Gideon, in return for all the good he'd done for Israel.
Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to see his mother's brothers. He spoke to them and to his mother's whole family.
“Ask the people of Shechem what's better for them: having all seventy of Jerubbaal's sons rule over them, or having just one ruler. And remember, I'm your own flesh and blood.”
His uncles repeated what he'd said to the men of Shechem. The men leaned toward Abimelech because they said, “He's one of us.”
They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal Berith. Abimelech used the money to hire a gang of reckless men who followed him.
He went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerubbaal, on a single stone. But Jerubbaal's youngest son, Jotham, survived because he hid.
All the men of Shechem and the whole house of Millo gathered and crowned Abimelech king by the oak beside the pillar at Shechem.
When Jotham heard, he went up to the top of Mount Gerizim and shouted, “Listen to me, people of Shechem, so God may listen to you.
The trees went looking for someone to anoint as king. They said to the olive tree, ‘Rule over us.’
The olive tree answered, ‘Should I give up my oil, which people use to honor God and others, just so I can wave above the trees?’
The trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come rule over us.’
The fig tree answered, ‘Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit just so I can wave above the trees?’
The trees said to the grapevine, ‘Come rule over us.’
The vine answered, ‘Should I give up my new wine, which brings cheer to God and people, just so I can wave above the trees?’
Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, ‘Come rule over us.’
The thornbush told them, ‘If you really mean to anoint me your king, come and shelter in my shade. If you don't, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’
Now, did you act honestly and fairly when you made Abimelech king? Did you treat Jerubbaal and his family well and give him what his actions deserved?
My father fought for you. He risked his life and rescued you from Midian.
Today you've turned against my father's family, killed his seventy sons on a single stone, and made Abimelech, his servant woman's son, king over Shechem because he's related to you.
If you truly treated Jerubbaal and his household honestly and fairly today, then find joy in Abimelech, and let him find joy in you.
Otherwise, may fire come from Abimelech and consume the people of Shechem and the house of Millo. And may fire come from Shechem and the house of Millo and consume Abimelech.”
Jotham then ran away to Beer and lived there because he was afraid of his brother Abimelech.
Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years.
Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and they turned against him.
This happened so the violence done to Jerubbaal's seventy sons would come back on Abimelech, their brother who killed them, and on the men of Shechem who helped him.
The men of Shechem set up ambushes in the hills against him and robbed people traveling along the road. Abimelech heard what they were doing.
Gaal son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his brothers, and the men of Shechem put their trust in him.
They went out to gather grapes and tread them, then celebrated. They went into their god's temple, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who are we in Shechem that we should serve him? Isn't he Jerubbaal's son, with Zebul as his officer? Serve the people of Hamor, Shechem's father. Why should we serve Abimelech?”
“If only I were in charge of these people, I'd get rid of Abimelech!” He challenged Abimelech, “Gather a bigger army and come out!”
When Zebul, the city's ruler, heard what Gaal son of Ebed had said, he burned with anger.
He secretly sent messengers to Abimelech. “Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem and are stirring up the city against you.
Bring your men up by night and wait in the fields.
Get up at sunrise and rush the city. When Gaal and his men come out against you, deal with them as the opportunity allows.”
Abimelech and all his men went up that night, split into four groups, and lay in wait outside Shechem.
Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the city gate. Abimelech and his men came out of hiding.
When Gaal saw them, he told Zebul, “Look! People are coming down from the hilltops.” Zebul said, “You're seeing shadows on the hills and mistaking them for people.”
Gaal spoke again. “Look, people are coming down through the middle of the land, and another group is coming by the oak of Meonenim.”
Zebul told him, “Where's your big talk now? You said, ‘Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?’ Those are the people you looked down on. Go out and fight them now.”
Gaal led the men of Shechem out to fight Abimelech.
Abimelech chased Gaal, and Gaal ran from him. Many fell wounded all the way back to the city gate.
Abimelech stayed at Arumah. Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem and kept them from living there.
The next day the people went out into the fields, and Abimelech heard about it.
He divided his men into three groups and waited in the fields. When he saw people coming out of the city, he rose up against them and attacked.
Abimelech and the groups with him rushed the city gate and took their stand there, while the other two groups charged against the people in the fields and struck them down.
Abimelech fought the city all day. He captured it, killed the people there, tore it down, and scattered salt over it.
When the people of Shechem's tower heard, they took refuge in the stronghold of the temple of Elberith.
Word reached Abimelech that all the people of Shechem's tower were gathered there.
Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon with his men, chopped a branch off a tree, and lifted it onto his shoulder. He told the men with him, “Quick, do what you just saw me do!”
Each man cut a branch and followed Abimelech. They put the branches against the stronghold and set it on fire. About a thousand men and women from Shechem's tower died.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez, camped against it, and captured it.
There was a strong tower inside the city. The men and women fled there, locked themselves in, and climbed to the roof.
Abimelech attacked the tower and came close to the entrance to burn it.
A woman threw an upper millstone down onto Abimelech and broke his skull.
He quickly called his young armor-bearer. “Draw your sword and kill me so nobody can say a woman killed me.” The young man ran him through, and he died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone went home.
That's how God paid Abimelech back for the evil he'd done to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
God also brought all the evil the men of Shechem had done back on their own heads. The curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal fell on them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, rose up to rescue Israel. He was from the tribe of Issachar and lived in Shamir in Ephraim's hill country.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.
After him came Jair from Gilead. He judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode thirty young donkeys. They had thirty towns in Gilead that are still called Havvoth Jair today.
Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

Again the Israelites did what was evil in the LORD's sight. They served the Baals, the Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines. They abandoned the LORD and stopped serving him.
The LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites.
That year they began crushing and oppressing the Israelites. For eighteen years they oppressed all the Israelites east of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites.
The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim too. Israel was in terrible distress.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD, “We've sinned against you by abandoning our God and serving the Baals.”
The LORD answered the Israelites, “Didn't I rescue you from the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, and Philistines?
The Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites oppressed you too. You cried out to me, and I rescued you from them.
But you've abandoned me and served other gods. So I won't rescue you anymore.
Go cry out to the gods you've chosen. Let them rescue you now that you're in trouble!”
The Israelites told the LORD, “We've sinned. Do whatever you think is right with us. Just please rescue us today.”
They got rid of their foreign gods and served the LORD, and Israel's misery grieved him.
Then the Ammonites gathered and set up camp in Gilead, while the Israelites gathered and camped at Mizpah.
The leaders of Gilead asked one another, “Who will lead the fight against the Ammonites? Whoever does it will become the leader of all who live in Gilead.”
Jephthah from Gilead was a brave warrior. His mother was a sex worker, and his father was Gilead.
Gilead's wife also had sons. When they grew up, they drove Jephthah away and told him, “You won't inherit anything in our father's household. You're the son of another woman.”
Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob. Outlaws gathered around him and went out with him.
Some time later the Ammonites went to war against Israel.
When that happened, the elders of Gilead went to the land of Tob to bring Jephthah back.
They told him, “Come be our commander so we can fight the Ammonites.”
Jephthah said, “Weren't you the ones who hated me and drove me out of my father's house? Why come to me now that you're in trouble?”
The elders replied, “That's why we've come back to you. Come with us to fight the Ammonites, and you'll lead everyone who lives in Gilead.”
Jephthah asked them, “If you bring me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD hands them over to me, will I really be your leader?”
The elders answered, “The LORD is our witness. We'll do exactly what you say.”
Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their leader and commander. He repeated the whole agreement before the LORD at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of Ammon. “What's your grievance with me? Why have you come to attack my land?”
The king of Ammon answered, “When Israel came up out of Egypt, they took my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. Give the territory back now, and we can settle this peacefully.”
Jephthah sent messengers back to the king of Ammon.
He said, “This is Jephthah's answer: Israel took neither Moab's land nor the land of the Ammonites.
When Israel came up from Egypt, they went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and reached Kadesh.
Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom asking permission to cross his land, but he wouldn't listen. Israel asked the king of Moab too, but he refused. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.
Then they traveled through the wilderness around Edom and Moab. They came along Moab's eastern side and camped across the Arnon. They didn't enter Moab, because the Arnon marked its border.
Israel sent messengers to King Sihon of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon. They said, ‘Please let us pass through your land to get where we're going.’
Sihon didn't trust Israel to cross his border. Instead, he gathered his people, camped at Jahaz, and fought Israel.
The LORD, the God of Israel, handed Sihon and all his people over to Israel, and Israel defeated them. Then Israel took possession of the country where the Amorites had lived.
They took all the Amorite territory, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
The LORD, the God of Israel, drove the Amorites out ahead of his people Israel. What makes you think you should take their land now?
Wouldn't you take whatever Chemosh your god gave you? We'll take the land of whoever the LORD our God drives out ahead of us.
Are you any better than King Balak of Moab, son of Zippor? Did he ever quarrel with Israel over this or fight against them?
Israel has lived in Heshbon and its towns, Aroer and its towns, and all the towns along the Arnon for three hundred years. Why didn't you take them back in all that time?
I've done you no wrong. You're the one wronging me by making war on me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between Israel and Ammon.”
The king of Ammon refused to listen to Jephthah's message.
Then the LORD's Spirit came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh, went through Mizpah in Gilead, and from there went toward the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the LORD. “If you really hand the Ammonites over to me,
then whatever comes out of my door to meet me when I return safely from Ammon will belong to the LORD, and I'll offer it as a burnt offering.”
Jephthah went over to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD handed them over to him.
He struck them down from Aroer to Minnith, twenty towns in all, and as far as Abelcheramim. It was a great slaughter, and the Ammonites were subdued before Israel.
When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, his daughter came out to meet him, dancing to tambourines. She was his only child. He had no other son or daughter.
When he saw her, he tore his clothes. “Oh, my daughter! You've brought me to my knees and become a source of grief to me. I gave the LORD my word, and I can't take it back.”
She said, “Father, you gave the LORD your word. Do to me what you promised, now that the LORD has taken vengeance for you on your enemies, the Ammonites.”
Then she asked her father for one thing. “Give me two months to go into the mountains with my friends and mourn that I'll never marry.”
“Go,” he said. He let her go for two months. She and her friends went into the mountains and mourned that she would remain a virgin.
After two months she came back to her father, and he carried out the vow he'd made. She had never slept with a man. It became a custom in Israel
for the women of Israel to go out four days each year to remember the daughter of Jephthah from Gilead.
The men of Ephraim gathered and crossed northward. They asked Jephthah, “Why did you cross over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We'll burn your house down with you inside!”
Jephthah answered, “My people and I were in a serious fight with the Ammonites. I called for your help, but you didn't rescue me from them.
When I saw you weren't coming, I risked my life and crossed over to fight the Ammonites. The LORD handed them over to me. So why have you come to fight me today?”

Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought Ephraim. The Gileadites defeated them because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are just fugitives from Ephraim, living among Ephraim and Manasseh.”
The Gileadites seized the Jordan crossings. Whenever an Ephraimite on the run asked to cross, the Gileadites asked, “Are you from Ephraim?” If the man answered no,

they told him, “Say ‘Shibboleth.’” When he said “Sibboleth” because he couldn't pronounce it the way they did, they seized him and killed him at the crossing. Forty-two thousand Ephraimites fell at that time.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then he died and was buried in one of the towns of Gilead.
After him, Ibzan from Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons. He gave his thirty daughters in marriage outside his clan and took thirty women from outside his clan as wives for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.
Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon from the tribe of Zebulun judged Israel for ten years.
Elon died and was buried at Aijalon in Zebulun's territory.
After him, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy young donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Abdon son of Hillel died and was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim's territory, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
The Israelites again did what was evil in the LORD's sight, and the LORD handed them over to the Philistines for forty years.
A man named Manoah lived in Zorah and belonged to the tribe of Dan. His wife was unable to have children.
The LORD's angel appeared to her and said, “You've been unable to have children, but you're going to become pregnant and give birth to a son.
Be careful now: don't drink wine or strong drink, and don't eat anything unclean.
You're going to give birth to a son. Never cut his hair, because the boy will be a Nazirite, set apart for God from the womb. He'll begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines.”
The woman went and told her husband, “A man of God came to me. His face looked like the face of God's angel. It was overwhelming. I didn't ask where he came from, and he didn't tell me his name.

But he told me, ‘You're going to become pregnant and give birth to a son. Don't drink wine or strong drink, and don't eat anything unclean. The boy will be a Nazirite, set apart for God from the womb until the day he dies.’”
Manoah prayed to the LORD, “Please, Lord, let the man of God you sent come back and teach us what to do for the boy who will be born.”
God listened to Manoah, and God's angel came back to the woman while she was sitting in the field. Her husband wasn't with her.
She ran to tell her husband, “Look! The man who came to me the other day has appeared again!”
Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he reached the man, he asked, “Are you the one who spoke to my wife?” He answered, “I am.”
Manoah said, “May what you've said come true. How is the boy to live, and what is he to do?”
The LORD's angel told Manoah, “Your wife must take care to do everything I told her.
She mustn't eat anything from the grapevine, drink wine or strong drink, or eat anything unclean. She must follow everything I commanded her.”
Manoah said to the LORD's angel, “Please stay while we prepare a young goat for you.”
The LORD's angel answered, “Even if I stay, I won't eat your food. If you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.” Manoah didn't yet realize he was the LORD's angel.
Manoah asked, “What's your name? We want to honor you when what you've said comes true.”
The LORD's angel answered, “Why do you ask my name? It's beyond what you can understand.”
So Manoah took the young goat and the grain offering and offered them to the LORD on the rock. Then the angel did something amazing while Manoah and his wife watched.
As the flames rose from the altar toward the sky, the LORD's angel rose in the flames. Manoah and his wife saw it and fell facedown to the ground.
The LORD's angel didn't appear to Manoah or his wife again. Then Manoah realized who he was.
Manoah told his wife, “We're sure to die. We've seen God.”
His wife said, “If the LORD had wanted to kill us, he wouldn't have accepted our burnt offering and grain offering. He wouldn't have shown us all these things or told us what he just did.”
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. He grew up, and the LORD blessed him.
The LORD's Spirit began to stir in him at Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and saw a Philistine woman there.
When he came back, he told his parents, “I saw a Philistine woman in Timnah. Get her for me as my wife.”

His parents asked, “Isn't there a woman among your relatives or anywhere among our people? Do you have to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson told his father, “Get her for me. She's the one I want.”
His parents didn't know this was from the LORD, who was looking for an occasion to act against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When they reached the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion came at him roaring.
The LORD's Spirit came powerfully upon Samson, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as easily as a young goat. He didn't tell his parents what he'd done.
He went down and talked with the woman, and he liked her very much.
Later he went back to marry her. On the way he turned aside to look at the dead lion and saw a swarm of bees and honey inside its body.
He scooped up the honey with his hands and ate as he walked. When he caught up with his parents, he gave them some too. They ate it, but he didn't tell them where he'd gotten it.
Samson's father went down to see the woman, and Samson held a feast there, as young men used to do.
When the people saw him, they brought thirty men to be his companions.
Samson said, “Let me give you a riddle. If you can solve it and tell me the answer within the seven days of the feast, I'll give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.
If you can't solve it, you owe me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.” They answered, “Go on. Let's hear the riddle.”
He said, “From the eater came food. From the strong came sweetness.” Three days went by, and they still couldn't solve it.
On the seventh day they told Samson's wife, “Get your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we'll burn you and your father's household. Did you invite us here to take everything we have?”

Samson's wife cried in front of him. “You hate me. You don't love me at all. You gave my people a riddle and haven't told me the answer.” He said, “I haven't even told my father or mother. Why should I tell you?”
She cried in front of him through the seven days of the feast. On the seventh day, she pressed him so hard that he told her. She passed the answer on to her people.

Before sunset on the seventh day, the men of the city told him, “What's sweeter than honey? What's stronger than a lion?” He answered, “If you hadn't plowed with my heifer, you never would've solved my riddle.”

The LORD's Spirit came powerfully upon him. He went down to Ashkelon, struck down thirty men, and took what they had. He gave the clothes to the men who'd answered his riddle. Furious, he went back to his father's house.
Samson's wife was given in marriage to the man who'd been his friend and companion at the wedding.
Some time later, during the wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat and went to see his wife. He said, “I'm going to my wife's room,” but her father wouldn't let him in.
Her father said, “I was sure you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Isn't her younger sister even more beautiful? Please take her instead.”
Samson told them, “This time nobody can blame me for what I do to the Philistines.”
Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes. He paired them tail to tail, with a torch between each pair.
He lit the torches and let the foxes loose in the Philistines' fields. The fire burned the standing grain, the harvested bundles, and the olive groves.

The Philistines asked, “Who did this?” They were told, “Samson, the Timnite's son-in-law, because the man gave Samson's wife to his companion.” So the Philistines came and burned her and her father to death.
Samson told them, “Since you've done this, I'll take revenge on you, and then I'll stop.”
He struck them down in a brutal slaughter. Then he went down to live in the cave at the Rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up, camped in Judah, and spread out at Lehi.
The men of Judah asked, “Why have you come against us?” The Philistines answered, “We've come to tie up Samson and do to him what he did to us.”

Three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave at the Rock of Etam and asked Samson, “Don't you know the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?” He said, “I only did to them what they did to me.”
They told him, “We've come to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson said, “Swear you won't attack me yourselves.”
They said, “We'll tie you up and hand you over, but we won't kill you ourselves.” They tied him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

When Samson reached Lehi, the Philistines came toward him shouting. Then the LORD's Spirit came powerfully upon him. The ropes around his arms were like flax burned in a fire, and his bonds fell from his hands.
He picked up a fresh donkey's jawbone and struck down a thousand men with it.
Samson said, “With a donkey's jawbone, heaps upon heaps. With a donkey's jawbone I've struck down a thousand men.”
When he finished speaking, he threw the jawbone away. That place was called Ramath Lehi.
Samson was extremely thirsty, so he called out to the LORD. “You've given your servant this great victory. Am I going to die of thirst now and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
God split open the hollow at Lehi, and water came out. Samson drank, got his strength back, and revived. That's why the spring is called En Hakkore. It's still in Lehi today.
Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
Samson went to Gaza, saw a sex worker there, and went in to see her.
Word got around Gaza that Samson was there. The people surrounded the place and waited quietly at the city gate all night. They said, “At daybreak we'll kill him.”
Samson stayed until midnight. Then he got up, pulled up the city gate with both posts and the crossbar, hoisted it onto his shoulders, and carried it to the top of the hill opposite Hebron.
Later he fell in love with a woman named Delilah in the Valley of Sorek.
The Philistine rulers came to her and said, “Coax him into telling you the source of his strength and how we can overpower and tie him up. Each of us will pay you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me where your great strength comes from and how someone could tie you up and overpower you.”
Samson said, “If I'm tied with seven fresh cords that haven't dried, I'll be as weak as anyone else.”
The Philistine rulers brought Delilah seven fresh cords, and she tied him with them.
With men waiting in the next room, she cried, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He snapped the cords like flax thread touching a flame. The secret of his strength stayed hidden.
Delilah said, “You've made a fool of me and lied to me. Please tell me how you can be tied up.”
He said, “If they tie me with brand-new ropes that have never been used, I'll be as weak as anyone else.”
Delilah tied him with new ropes and cried, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” Men were waiting in the inner room, but Samson snapped the ropes off his arms like thread.
Delilah said, “You've been making a fool of me and lying this whole time. Tell me how you can be tied up.” He said, “If you weave the seven braids of my hair into the cloth on the loom.”
She fastened the cloth with the pin and shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He woke up and pulled out the loom's pin and the cloth.
She told him, “How can you say you love me when you won't trust me? You've made a fool of me three times and still haven't told me where your strength comes from.”
She pressed him day after day until he was worn down to the point of death.

He finally told her everything. “My hair has never been cut. I've been a Nazirite, set apart for God since before I was born. If my head is shaved, I'll lose my strength and be as weak as anyone else.”
Delilah realized he'd told her everything. She sent for the Philistine rulers: “Come back one more time. He's told me the whole truth.” They came with the silver.
She got Samson to fall asleep in her lap and called for a man to shave off his seven braids. She began to overpower him, and his strength left him.
She cried, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He woke up and thought, “I'll get out of this like I always do. I'll shake myself free.” He didn't know the LORD had left him.
The Philistines seized him, put out his eyes, and took him down to Gaza. They bound him in bronze shackles and made him grind grain in prison.
But the hair on his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
The Philistine rulers gathered to offer a big sacrifice to their god Dagon and celebrate. They said, “Our god has handed our enemy Samson over to us.”
When the people saw Samson, they praised their god. “Our god has handed us the enemy who devastated our land and killed so many of us.”
In high spirits they said, “Bring Samson out to entertain us.” They brought him out of prison, and he performed for them. They stood him between the pillars.
Samson told the boy holding his hand, “Let me feel the pillars that hold the building up so I can lean against them.”
The building was full of men and women, including all the Philistine rulers. About three thousand men and women were on the roof watching Samson perform.
Samson called out to the LORD: “Lord GOD, please remember me. Please give me strength just one more time, God, so I can get even with the Philistines for taking my eyes.”
Samson braced himself between the two middle pillars that supported the building, one on either side of him.

He said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He pushed with all his strength, and the building came down on the rulers and everyone inside. Samson killed more people in his death than he had in his life.

His brothers and his father's whole household came down to take his body. They brought him back and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He judged Israel for twenty years.
There was a man named Micah who lived in the hill country of Ephraim.

He told his mother, “Remember the eleven hundred pieces of silver that were stolen from you? I heard you put a curse on whoever took them. I have the silver. I took it.” His mother said, “May the LORD bless you, my son!”
He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver. His mother said, “I'm dedicating this silver to the LORD for my son, to make a carved image and a cast image. So I'll give it back to you.”
When he returned the money to his mother, she gave two hundred pieces of silver to a silversmith. He made a carved image and a cast image, and they were kept in Micah's house.
Micah had a shrine. He made an ephod and household idols, and he appointed one of his sons to be his priest.
In those days Israel had no king. Everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes.
A young Levite was living in Bethlehem in Judah, among the clans of Judah.
He left Bethlehem to find somewhere else to live. As he traveled through Ephraim's hill country, he came to Micah's house.
Micah asked him, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I'm a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah. I'm looking for a place to live.”
Micah told him, “Stay with me and be a father and priest to me. I'll give you ten pieces of silver a year, a set of clothes, and your food.” So the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to stay, and the young man became like one of Micah's own sons.
Micah appointed him as priest, and the young Levite became his priest and lived in his house.
Then Micah said, “Now I know the LORD will bless me, because I have a Levite for my priest.”
In those days Israel had no king. The tribe of Dan was looking for land to settle in, because up to that time they hadn't received an inheritance among Israel's tribes.

The Danites picked five capable men from their clans in Zorah and Eshtaol and sent them to scout the land. “Go explore it,” they said. The men reached Ephraim's hill country and stayed at Micah's house.
Near Micah's house they recognized the young Levite's voice. They went over and asked, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What do you have here?”
He told them what Micah had done for him and said, “He hired me, and I've become his priest.”
They asked, “Please ask God whether our journey will go well.”
The priest said, “Go in peace. The LORD is watching over the road you're taking.”

The five men went on to Laish. They saw people living quietly and securely, like the Sidonians. There was no one in the land with power to oppress them. They were a long way from Sidon and had no dealings with anyone else.
When the men came back to their relatives in Zorah and Eshtaol, their relatives asked, “What did you find?”
They answered, “Get up. Let's go against them. We've seen the land, and it's very good. Why are you still sitting there? Don't put off going in and taking possession of it.
When you get there, you'll find unsuspecting people and a wide stretch of land. God has handed it over to you, a place that has everything you could need.”
Six hundred Danite men armed for war set out from Zorah and Eshtaol.
They went up and camped at Kiriath Jearim in Judah. That's why the place behind Kiriath Jearim is still called Mahaneh Dan today.
From there they went through Ephraim's hill country and reached Micah's house.
The five men who had scouted Laish told the others, “Did you know these houses have an ephod, household idols, a carved image, and a cast image? Think about what you're going to do.”
They turned aside to Micah's house, where the young Levite lived, and asked how he was doing.
The six hundred armed men from Dan stayed by the entrance to the gate.
The five scouts went inside and took the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast image. The priest stood by the gate with the six hundred armed men.
When they went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast image, the priest asked, “What are you doing?”
They said, “Keep quiet. Put your hand over your mouth and come with us. Be a father and priest to us. Would you rather be priest to one man's household or to a whole tribe and clan in Israel?”
The priest was glad to hear it. He took the ephod, the household idols, and the carved image and went with them.
They turned and left, putting their children, livestock, and belongings ahead of them.
When they'd gone some distance from Micah's house, the men who lived near him gathered and caught up with the Danites.
They shouted after the Danites, who turned around and asked Micah, “What's wrong with you? Why have you come with all these men?”
Micah said, “You took the gods I made and my priest, and then you walked off! What have I got left? How can you ask me what's wrong?”
The Danites told him, “Don't let us hear another word from you. Some of these men might lose their temper and attack you. You and your household could lose your lives.”
The Danites went on their way. When Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned around and went home.
The Danites took what Micah had made and the priest who had served him. They went to Laish, where the people were quiet and unsuspecting, put them to the sword, and burned the city.
Nobody came to rescue Laish. It was far from Sidon, and its people had no dealings with anyone else. It lay in the valley near Beth Rehob. The Danites rebuilt the city and settled there.
They named it Dan after their ancestor Dan, one of Israel's sons. The city used to be called Laish.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the land went into captivity.
They kept Micah's carved image set up for themselves all the time God's house was at Shiloh.
In those days Israel had no king. A Levite living in a remote part of Ephraim's hill country took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
She was unfaithful to him, left him, and went back to her father's house in Bethlehem. She stayed there four months.
Her husband went after her to speak kindly to her and bring her back. He took his servant and two donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and her father was glad to see him.
His father-in-law persuaded him to stay. He spent three days there, eating, drinking, and sleeping at the house.
On the fourth day they got up early, and the man prepared to leave. His father-in-law said, “Have a bite of bread to give you strength. Then you can go.”
So the two sat down and ate and drank together. Then the woman's father told him, “Please stay one more night and enjoy yourself.”
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law urged him to stay, so he spent another night there.
On the fifth morning he got up early to leave. The woman's father said, “Please eat something and stay until later in the day.” So the two of them ate.

When the man got up to leave with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law said, “It's nearly evening. Please stay the night. The day's almost over. Enjoy yourself here, then get an early start home tomorrow.”
This time the man refused to spend the night. He got up and traveled as far as Jebus, also called Jerusalem. His two saddled donkeys and his concubine went with him.
By the time they reached Jebus, the day was nearly over. The servant told his master, “Let's go into this Jebusite city and stay the night.”
His master answered, “We won't go into a foreign city where the people aren't Israelites. We'll go on to Gibeah.”
He told his servant, “Come on, let's reach one of these towns. We'll spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah.”
So they kept going. The sun went down as they reached Gibeah, which belonged to Benjamin.
They turned into Gibeah to spend the night. The man went in and sat down in the open square, because no one invited them home to stay.
That evening an old man came in from working in the fields. He was from Ephraim's hill country and was living in Gibeah, but the people of the town were Benjaminites.
When he looked up and saw the traveler in the square, he asked, “Where are you going? Where did you come from?”

The man answered, “We're traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to a remote part of Ephraim's hill country. That's where I'm from. I went to Bethlehem, and now I'm going to the LORD's house, but nobody has taken me in.
We have straw and feed for the donkeys, and bread and wine for me, the woman with me, and my young servant. We have everything we need.”
The old man said, “Peace to you. Let me take care of whatever you need. Just don't spend the night in the square.”
He brought them into his house and fed their donkeys. They washed their feet, then ate and drank.

As they were enjoying themselves, some wicked men from the town surrounded the house and beat on the door. They demanded of the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came to your house. We want to rape him.”
The owner went outside and said, “Please, my brothers, don't do something so wicked. This man is a guest in my house. Don't do this terrible thing.
My daughter, who's a virgin, is here, and so is his concubine. I'll bring them out. You can abuse them and do whatever you want to them, but don't do this terrible thing to the man.”
The men refused to listen. So the Levite seized his concubine and pushed her outside to them. They raped and abused her all night, then let her go at dawn.
At daybreak the woman came back to the house where her husband was staying. She collapsed at the door and lay there until it was light.
Her husband got up in the morning, opened the doors, and went out to leave. There she lay at the entrance, her hands on the doorstep.
He said, “Get up. Let's go.” She didn't answer. He lifted her onto the donkey and set out for home.
When he reached his house, he cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout Israel.
Everyone who saw what had happened said, “Nothing like this has been done or seen since the Israelites came out of Egypt. Think about it, talk it over, and speak up.”
The Israelites came together as one community before the LORD at Mizpah, from Dan to Beersheba and from Gilead.
The leaders of all Israel's tribes took their places in the assembly of God's people. There were four hundred thousand foot soldiers armed with swords.
The people of Benjamin heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites asked, “Tell us how this terrible thing happened.”
The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered, “My concubine and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
The men of Gibeah came after me and surrounded the house at night. They meant to kill me. They raped my concubine, and she died.
I cut her body into pieces and sent them throughout the land Israel inherited, because these men did something vile and outrageous in Israel.
Now all of you are Israelites. Tell us here what you think we should do.”
The people rose together and said, “None of us will go back to our tents or return to our homes.
Here's what we'll do to Gibeah. We'll cast lots to determine who goes up against it.

We'll assign ten men out of every hundred, a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand across Israel's tribes to get food for the people. Then the others can follow through at Gibeah in Benjamin for the outrage its people committed in Israel.”
So the Israelites gathered against the city, united as one.
Israel's tribes sent men throughout Benjamin to ask, “What is this evil that's happened among you?
Hand over the wicked men in Gibeah so we can put them to death and remove this evil from Israel.” But Benjamin refused to listen to their fellow Israelites.
The Benjaminites came together from their towns at Gibeah to fight against Israel.
That day the towns of Benjamin counted twenty-six thousand swordsmen, plus seven hundred chosen men from Gibeah.
Among these soldiers were seven hundred chosen left-handed men. Every one could sling a stone at a hair without missing.
Apart from Benjamin, Israel counted four hundred thousand men armed with swords, all ready for battle.
The Israelites went up to Bethel and asked God, “Which tribe should go up first to fight Benjamin?” The LORD answered, “Judah first.”
In the morning the Israelites got up and camped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel went out to fight Benjamin and took up their positions at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and struck down twenty-two thousand Israelites that day.
Israel's men encouraged one another and formed their battle line again where they'd stood the first day.
They went up and wept before the LORD until evening. They asked, “Should we go back to fight our relatives from Benjamin?” The LORD answered, “Go up against them.”
On the second day the Israelites went out against Benjamin again.
Benjamin came out of Gibeah on the second day and struck down another eighteen thousand Israelites, all armed with swords.
Then all the Israelites went up to Bethel. They sat there weeping in the LORD's presence and fasted until evening. Then they brought burnt offerings and peace offerings before him.
The Israelites asked the LORD for guidance. God's ark of the covenant was there at the time,

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, served before it. They asked, “Should we go out again to fight our relatives from Benjamin, or should we stop?” The LORD answered, “Go up. Tomorrow I'll hand them over to you.”
Israel set ambushes around Gibeah.
On the third day the Israelites went up against Benjamin and lined up for battle at Gibeah, just as before.
Benjamin came out against them and was drawn away from the city. They started striking down Israelites as before, in the fields and on the roads to Bethel and Gibeah. They killed about thirty men.
The Benjaminites said, “We're beating them just like the first time.” But the Israelites had planned to retreat and draw them away from the city onto the roads.
Israel's main force regrouped at Baal Tamar. Israel's men in hiding also rushed out from Maareh Geba.
Ten thousand chosen men from across Israel came against Gibeah. The fighting was fierce, and the Benjaminites didn't realize disaster was about to hit them.
The LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel. That day the Israelites struck down twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin, all armed with swords.
Then the Benjaminites realized they'd been beaten. The men of Israel had given ground because they relied on the men they'd stationed outside Gibeah.
The men in hiding rushed into Gibeah, spread through the city, and put it to the sword.
Israel's men had agreed that a great cloud of smoke rising from the city would be the signal from the men in hiding.
When Israel's men fell back during the battle, Benjamin began striking them down and killed about thirty. The Benjaminites thought, “We're beating them just like in the first battle.”
Then a column of smoke began to rise. The Benjaminites looked back and saw the whole city going up in smoke.
Israel's men turned on them. The Benjaminites panicked when they saw that disaster had overtaken them.
They fled from Israel toward the wilderness, but the fighting followed close behind. The men coming out of the towns struck them down in the middle of it.
The Israelites surrounded Benjamin, chased them, and struck them down at their resting place as far as the area east of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all able warriors.
The rest fled toward the Rock of Rimmon in the wilderness. Israel struck down five thousand on the roads and pursued them to Gidom, where they struck down two thousand more.
In all, twenty-five thousand swordsmen of Benjamin fell that day. Every one was a warrior.
Six hundred men escaped to the Rock of Rimmon in the wilderness and stayed there four months.
The Israelites turned back against Benjamin and put to the sword everyone they found in the city, along with the livestock. They set fire to every town they came across.
The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, “None of us will give his daughter in marriage to a man from Benjamin.”
The people went to Bethel and sat before God until evening. They cried out and wept bitterly.
They said, “LORD, God of Israel, why has this happened? How can Israel be missing a whole tribe today?”
The next morning the people got up early and built an altar there. They brought burnt offerings and peace offerings.

The Israelites asked, “Who among all the tribes of Israel didn't come to the assembly before the LORD?” They'd sworn a solemn oath that anyone who failed to come before the LORD at Mizpah would be put to death.
The Israelites grieved for their relatives in Benjamin and said, “A whole tribe has been cut off from Israel today.
How will we find wives for the survivors? We've sworn by the LORD to give them none of our daughters in marriage.”
They asked again, “Which people from Israel's tribes didn't come before the LORD at Mizpah?” It turned out nobody from Jabesh Gilead had come to the camp for the assembly.
When they counted the people, they found no one there from Jabesh Gilead.
The assembly sent twelve thousand of their best fighters and ordered them to put the people of Jabesh Gilead to the sword, including women and children.
They were told to kill every male and every woman who had slept with a man.
They found four hundred young women in Jabesh Gilead who had never slept with a man and brought them to the camp at Shiloh in Canaan.
The whole assembly then sent word to the Benjaminites at the Rock of Rimmon and offered them peace.
The Benjaminites came back, and the Israelites gave them the women they'd spared from Jabesh Gilead. There still weren't enough women for all of them.
The people grieved for Benjamin because the LORD had opened a gap among the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the assembly asked, “How can we find wives for the men who are left? The women of Benjamin have been killed.”
They said, “The survivors of Benjamin must have an inheritance so that a tribe isn't erased from Israel.
But we can't give them our daughters as wives, because Israel swore that anyone who gives Benjamin a wife would be cursed.”
Then they remembered the LORD's yearly festival in Shiloh. Shiloh is north of Bethel, east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.
They told the men of Benjamin to wait in the vineyards.
They told them to watch for the young women of Shiloh who came out to dance, seize them as wives, and take them back to Benjamin's territory.

They said that if the women's fathers or brothers complained, they'd ask them to let it stand. They hadn't secured a wife for each man in battle, and the families hadn't given the women away and so hadn't broken the oath.
The Benjaminites did as they were told. They carried off enough women from the dancers to take as wives. Then they returned to their inheritance, rebuilt the towns, and settled in them.
The other Israelites left too, each returning to their own tribe, clan, and inheritance.
In those days Israel had no king. Everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes.
